title: The Janitor Always Mops Twice

jokes.text: That poor sap doing the two-step to nowhere is me. Bet you're wondering how I got into this mess.
jokes.setup: Classic noir voiceover opening — Charlie narrating over what is presumably himself in distress
jokes.punchline: The 'two-step to nowhere' is a deliberately overwrought noir cliché delivered by Charlie, who is a janitor, making the grandiosity absurd
jokes.explanation: The joke is structural — Charlie playing a hard-boiled noir detective is inherently funny given his character. The earnestness sells it. Works as a premise-establisher with solid character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I suppose I should start at the end. My end, that is.

jokes.text: I needed a hospital, I needed a day off, I needed a pretty girl with soft lips and a nursing degree. What I had was a mop, a bucket, and a bellyful of regret.
jokes.setup: Noir narration builds to a list of romantic/desperate needs
jokes.punchline: The 'mop, bucket, and bellyful of regret' subverts the romantic noir list — he's just a janitor with janitor things
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the list of romantic needs vs. the janitor reality is perfectly calibrated. The 'bellyful of regret' keeps one foot in noir while the mop and bucket puncture it. Strong economy and character integration: only Charlie could make janitor tools feel this tragic.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That poor sap doing the two-step to nowhere is me.

jokes.text: So, how does an honest man end up spilling his guts on a dive bar floor? Don't ask me, pal. I'm just the janitor.
jokes.setup: Rhetorical noir question implying deep moral complexity
jokes.punchline: He deflects the grand question with 'I'm just the janitor' — the whole noir framing is undercut by his actual job
jokes.explanation: Clean, well-constructed joke. The pivot from 'honest man' philosophical musing to 'I'm just the janitor' is sharp and economic. The self-awareness is funny without being too winking.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: The victim? A handicap stall. The murderer? A butt. But whose butt?

jokes.text: See, that morning I got called to a crime scene in the men's bathroom. The victim? A handicap stall. The murderer? A butt. But whose butt? That, my friends, was the hundred-dollar question.
jokes.setup: Noir 'crime scene' setup with ominous language about a victim and murderer
jokes.punchline: The victim is a handicap stall. The murderer is a butt. Applied with complete noir seriousness to a bathroom mess.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The escalating noir phrasing — victim, murderer, hundred-dollar question — applied to bathroom destruction is perfectly executed. The reveal of 'A butt' as the murderer is delivered deadpan and lands hard. Only Charlie would apply this level of gravitas to fecal destruction. Highly quotable, strong craft on all axes.

dialogue.line: trouble walked in like it always does, on a great set of legs.

jokes.text: And that's when trouble walked in like it always does, on a great set of legs.
jokes.setup: Classic femme fatale noir entrance line
jokes.punchline: The 'great set of legs' belongs to Dee, who is not traditionally framed as a femme fatale — the disconnect is the joke
jokes.explanation: Solid use of the noir femme fatale trope applied to Dee, who is frequently the butt of physical jokes on the show. The setup is a bit conventional but the character-specific application gives it a boost.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Boy, has he got you trained. All that for a whistle? I wonder what you'd do for a biscuit.

jokes.text: Hey, Charlie, don't make me mop the floor with you, huh?
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to intimidate Charlie into mopping
jokes.punchline: The threat 'mop the floor with you' is a cliché fight idiom — but it's also literally what they want Charlie to do
jokes.explanation: Functional wordplay joke — the double meaning works in context. Not particularly original but executed efficiently.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't worry. In five minutes, he'll be up and chasing his tail again.

jokes.text: Boy, has he got you trained. All that for a whistle? I wonder what you'd do for a biscuit.
jokes.setup: Mac used a whistle to summon Charlie; Dee observes this
jokes.punchline: Dee compares Charlie to a trained dog — 'All that for a whistle? I wonder what you'd do for a biscuit'
jokes.explanation: Good character-specific insult — the Charlie-as-dog comparison fits the show's established dynamic. Economical and character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You know, they say any port in a storm, and this port just... Ah, shit, it's you!

jokes.text: Don't worry. In five minutes, he'll be up and chasing his tail again.
jokes.setup: Mac presumably just physically punished Charlie for the biscuit comment
jokes.punchline: Mac continues the dog metaphor by saying Charlie will be 'up and chasing his tail again'
jokes.explanation: Extension of the dog comparison gag. Less fresh than the original since it repeats the same metaphor, but the continuation works in context.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He's been diarrhea-poisoned.

jokes.text: The handsome bartender? Or the mop jockey in the coveralls?
jokes.setup: Mac threatens Charlie about the private party — implies if the floors aren't clean, someone gets blamed
jokes.punchline: He calls himself 'the handsome bartender' with complete sincerity, the self-aggrandizement being the joke
jokes.explanation: Mac's narcissism is perfectly channeled here — calling himself 'the handsome bartender' is pure Mac. Strong character integration for a quick line.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: He's absolutely carpet-bombed my bathroom. And my carpet.

jokes.text: Well, hello, sweetheart. You know, they say any port in a storm, and this port just... Ah, shit, it's you!
jokes.setup: Charlie hears someone enter and launches into a noir romantic greeting, clearly expecting a femme fatale
jokes.punchline: He sees who it actually is and immediately deflates — 'Ah, shit, it's you!'
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection with clean execution. The 'any port in a storm' buildup is punctured perfectly by 'Ah, shit, it's you!' The comedic timing implied in the transcript is sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Huh. Lot of that going around.

jokes.text: It's Frank. He's been diarrhea-poisoned.
jokes.setup: Dee arrives with urgent news delivered in full noir-messenger mode
jokes.punchline: 'Diarrhea-poisoned' — a Charlie-ism that is simultaneously specific and absurd
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout lines. 'Diarrhea-poisoned' is perfect — it's weirdly specific, delivered with complete gravitas by Dee playing messenger, and it's a pure Charlie-logic coinage that makes immediate sense while being totally absurd. The word 'poisoned' implies nefarious intent while 'diarrhea' makes it farcical. Highly quotable and immediately memorable.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm a knockout blonde with a body that would make a statue blush.

jokes.text: His words, not mine. He's stuck at my place. He's absolutely carpet-bombed my bathroom. And my carpet.
jokes.setup: Dee explains Frank's condition
jokes.punchline: 'Carpet-bombed my bathroom. And my carpet.' — the escalation to 'my carpet' adds the extra beat that makes it land
jokes.explanation: The 'And my carpet' tag is what makes this joke — it's the extra escalation beat that transforms a good line into a great one. The literal/military wordplay with 'carpet-bombed' applied to actual carpet is clean and efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I get more of a goon vibe from you.

jokes.text: Huh. Lot of that going around.
jokes.setup: Dee has just described Frank explosively soiling her bathroom and carpet
jokes.punchline: Charlie responds as if this is a mild, common occurrence — 'Lot of that going around'
jokes.explanation: Perfect deadpan economy — four words that do enormous comedic work. The casual acceptance of bathroom catastrophe as 'going around' like a cold is very Charlie. Also ties back to the crime scene in the men's bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Make it stiff enough to stand on its head and sing 'Oh! Susanna'.

jokes.text: No? I... I'm a knockout blonde with a body that would make a statue blush. I get more of a goon vibe from you.
jokes.setup: Charlie calls Dee a 'goon' in his noir framing; Dee protests by using an overly flattering self-description
jokes.punchline: The gap between Dee's self-image ('knockout blonde with a body that would make a statue blush') and her actual standing in the show is the joke; Charlie deflects right back
jokes.explanation: Dee's delusion about her own attractiveness is a classic character note. 'A body that would make a statue blush' is a deliberately overwrought noir phrase that she sincerely applies to herself, which is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: You can have tap.

jokes.text: Either I take the job, or you and the other goons play patty-cake with my kidneys.
jokes.setup: Charlie is narrating his noir 'choice' to take or refuse the job
jokes.punchline: 'Play patty-cake with my kidneys' — an absurdly childish euphemism for violence in a hard-boiled context
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of 'patty-cake' (a children's hand game) with 'kidneys' (physical violence) is a great absurdist image. It's a fresh spin on the 'work me over' cliché.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The rat bastard liquefied my guts

jokes.text: Hey, that's all you had to say. Let me get my hat.
jokes.setup: Dee negotiates through threats; finally offers Charlie a new set of rags
jokes.punchline: After all the elaborate noir posturing, Charlie immediately capitulates for 'rags' — his actual value system exposed
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie reveal — all the tough-guy posturing collapses for a set of cleaning rags. The gap between the noir persona and his actual motivations is a consistent and well-mined vein in this episode.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're giving off big goon vibes, Dee. Very goonish.

jokes.text: Make it stiff enough to stand on its head and sing 'Oh! Susanna'.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks for a drink before entering Frank's room
jokes.punchline: The drink specification — 'stiff enough to stand on its head and sing Oh! Susanna' — is hilariously overwrought and nonsensical
jokes.explanation: Brilliant absurdist riff on the classic noir 'make it a stiff one.' The image of a drink 'standing on its head and singing Oh! Susanna' is so specific and so weird that it becomes a great standalone line. Very quotable and pure Charlie.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Don't be a liar, Frankie-Boy, or your pants will catch on fire. Or they would, if you were wearing any pants.

jokes.text: You can have tap.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just made an elaborate, poetic request for a stiff drink
jokes.punchline: Dee's flat 'You can have tap' punctures the whole noir romanticism in three words
jokes.explanation: Perfect comic deflation. After Charlie's elaborate drink request, 'You can have tap' is a masterclass in comedic economy — maximum comedy per word. The indignity of tap water after that speech is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I found enough beef to open a hamburger store.

jokes.text: No, this morning you barged in here saying, 'They got me. I've been diarrhea-poisoned. The rat bastard liquefied my guts'.
jokes.setup: Frank claims he wasn't poisoned — just bad shrimp
jokes.punchline: Dee recounts Frank's exact dramatic words: 'The rat bastard liquefied my guts' — which contradicts his current denial
jokes.explanation: The 'liquefied my guts' callback expands the diarrhea-poisoned mythology. Frank's earlier panic and current denial create good irony, and the specific phrase 'the rat bastard liquefied my guts' is funny in its blend of noir slang and bodily horror.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm a janitor. Cleaning up messes is what I do.

jokes.text: Quit flapping your gums, goon!
jokes.setup: Dee is trying to participate in the conversation; Frank dismisses her
jokes.punchline: Frank calling Dee a 'goon' — she has been repeatedly saddled with this label throughout the episode
jokes.explanation: Part of the running gag of everyone calling Dee a goon. Less impactful on its own but feeds the pattern.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Her eyes glistened in the moonlight like fresh gasoline puddles.

jokes.text: Where were you when the brown lightning hit?
jokes.setup: Charlie interrogates Frank noir-style about the poisoning
jokes.punchline: 'Brown lightning' as a noir-sounding euphemism for explosive diarrhea — delivered with complete investigative seriousness
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. 'Brown lightning' sounds exactly like hardboiled noir slang but is actually a scatological euphemism. The delivery context — Charlie conducting a serious interrogation — makes it land perfectly. Highly quotable and original.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: They were the kind of eyes you could fall in... and summer in. And winter in, too.

jokes.text: Don't be a liar, Frankie-Boy, or your pants will catch on fire. Or they would, if you were wearing any pants.
jokes.setup: Charlie is interrogating Frank and suspects he's lying
jokes.punchline: Charlie riffs on 'liar liar pants on fire' — then reminds us Frank has no pants, which connects back to the established fact of Frank fleeing pantless
jokes.explanation: Smart callback that ties a children's rhyme to an established plot detail. The two-part structure — 'or they would, if you were wearing any pants' — earns a second laugh from the original setup. Good craft.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: My boyfriend looks like a bad apple, but once you get to know Vince, you'd like him even less.

jokes.text: Sorry, chum. You mess with the toilet, you get the janitor.
jokes.setup: Frank warns Charlie off the investigation
jokes.punchline: Charlie's tough-guy response riffs on 'you mess with the bull, you get the horns' — but it's about toilets and janitors
jokes.explanation: Very strong line. 'You mess with the toilet, you get the janitor' is a perfect subversion of the classic idiom that also doubles as the episode's thesis statement. Extremely character-specific and economical. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: You don't seem like the straightening type. Maybe 'cause you got me all twisted.

jokes.text: And, buddy, I found enough beef to open a hamburger store.
jokes.setup: Charlie narrates searching for people with grievances against Frank
jokes.punchline: The quantification of 'beef' (grievances) as enough to 'open a hamburger store' — an absurdly literal application of the slang
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie literalism — taking the slang word 'beef' and extending it to its literal meaning creates a funny image. The specificity of 'hamburger store' rather than 'steakhouse' or similar is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Yeah, there's no booze, no legal cooze. Sounds like a snooze. And there's barely any dudes.

jokes.text: Maybe the bad guy was hiding at the bottom of a beer bottle.
jokes.setup: Charlie heads to Paddy's looking for clues
jokes.punchline: The 'bad guy hiding at the bottom of a beer bottle' implies Charlie is just going to drink — the noir framing is a pretext
jokes.explanation: Good character note — the noir trope of the detective-who-drinks is applied to Charlie who would genuinely just drink. Efficient and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Cricket? What are you doing here?

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Dee paid me to cover her shift, hence the getup.

jokes.text: I should've swung my head into a beehive. It would've been safer than turning that corner.
jokes.setup: Charlie is about to encounter danger outside Paddy's
jokes.punchline: The danger is so bad he compares it unfavorably to swinging his head into a beehive — a bizarrely specific and vivid image
jokes.explanation: The beehive image is fresh and vivid — a good noir hyperbole with Charlie-specific absurdism. The specificity of 'swung my head' elevates it above generic danger-idioms.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: More. Oh, yes. Do it. Harder. Yes. I'm a slut.

jokes.text: Now dust, before I beat you like an old rug.
jokes.setup: Charlie intervenes in an assault, telling the thug to leave
jokes.punchline: 'Beat you like an old rug' — another cleaning metaphor used as a noir threat, consistent with janitor-as-detective theme
jokes.explanation: Consistent with the episode's janitor-noir theme — 'beat you like an old rug' is a cleaning metaphor that doubles as a threat. The 'dust' command (another cleaning word) adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: Frank hired me to go down to the local bars and stick my fingers in the garnish stations.

jokes.text: Her eyes glistened in the moonlight like fresh gasoline puddles. They were the kind of eyes you could fall in... and summer in. And winter in, too.
jokes.setup: Charlie spots the Waitress and launches into noir-romantic description
jokes.punchline: 'Like fresh gasoline puddles' subverts the romantic simile; then 'summer in and winter in too' escalates the absurdity of spending all seasons inside someone's eyes
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Fresh gasoline puddles' is a genuinely inspired subversion of the classic 'eyes like stars' simile — it's specific, visual, and deeply wrong in a way that feels right for Charlie's obsession. The escalating 'fall in, summer in, and winter in too' builds beautifully. This is exactly how the Charlie/Waitress dynamic gets comedy gold from his fixation.

dialogue.speaker: Cricket
dialogue.line: When someone flashes a roll of nickels at you, you don't ask questions, you just do.

jokes.text: Sorry about that. My boyfriend looks like a bad apple, but once you get to know Vince, you'd like him even less.
jokes.setup: The Waitress apologizes for her boyfriend Vince's behavior
jokes.punchline: 'Once you get to know Vince, you'd like him even less' — the structure implies she's about to defend him, then completely undercuts it
jokes.explanation: Excellent structure — the classic 'once you get to know them, you'd like them' is flipped perfectly. The delivery in the transcript is timed beautifully. High quotability, excellent economy, well-constructed misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Plus, I saw you put cat food in it.

jokes.text: You're too nice a girl to be playing with rotten apples. / Well, my pies haven't always been so sweet.
jokes.setup: Charlie and the Waitress trade noir-coded pleasantries about her bad relationship
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's response — 'my pies haven't always been so sweet' — is a coded admission delivered as a noir line, with pie being the ironic through-line of the episode
jokes.explanation: The pie metaphor is established here and pays off later when pies become the literal vehicle for poisoning. Gets a rewatch bonus for that reason. As a standalone the exchange is competent but not spectacular.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Maybe I did, maybe I didn't.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: You did, Charlie, I saw you scoop it out of the can...

jokes.text: Maybe 'cause you got me all twisted.
jokes.setup: The Waitress teases that Charlie doesn't seem like the 'straightening type'
jokes.punchline: 'Maybe 'cause you got me all twisted' — a noir-romantic line that also hints at Charlie's general mental state
jokes.explanation: Competent noir exchange with good character specificity. Charlie's romantic yearning for the Waitress is channeled into the noir vernacular in a way that feels earned.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Why are you smiling?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well, I'm trying to look sexy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're supposed to be dead.

jokes.text: No booze, no legal cooze. Sounds like a snooze.
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis complain about the private party — it's for a bigwig's daughter, not what they expected
jokes.punchline: Mac's rhyming complaint — 'no booze, no legal cooze, sounds like a snooze' — is both crass and weirdly rhythmic
jokes.explanation: The accidental rhyme scheme is mildly funny, and 'legal cooze' is a typically awful Mac phrase. Not particularly clever but consistent with the character.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You're not supposed to be sexy. You're supposed to be the goon.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm not the goddamn goon.

jokes.text: - And there's barely any dudes. - Don't add on. - There's a rhythm.
jokes.setup: Mac has just delivered a tidy rhyming complaint; Dennis tries to add a line
jokes.punchline: Mac criticizes Dennis for trying to add on — 'There's a rhythm' — breaking the fourth wall to comment on their own comedic structure
jokes.explanation: Smart meta moment — Mac defending the comedic integrity of his own rhyme scheme is very funny and self-aware without being too winking. 'There's a rhythm' is an unexpectedly sophisticated complaint from Mac.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: He gives us 30%, only Mac thinks it's ten.

jokes.text: Funny you should mention his guts, considering Frank got diarrhea-poisoned. In his guts.
jokes.setup: Mac says he hates Frank's guts
jokes.punchline: Charlie literally connects 'his guts' to the diarrhea poisoning — the clarification 'in his guts' is redundantly specific and funny
jokes.explanation: Good callback that also contains its own joke — the pedantic 'In his guts' clarification is funny because it's entirely unnecessary. Charlie's literalism shines.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You talking to me? Yeah. Well, I can't tell 'cause I'm not looking at you.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We ain't looking at you either.

jokes.text: Can I get a Red 40?
jokes.setup: Charlie is interrogating Mac and Dennis about the diarrhea poisoning
jokes.punchline: A child at the party innocently asks for 'a Red 40' — the dye at the center of the cherry conspiracy — without knowing what it means
jokes.explanation: Nicely planted — the audience doesn't yet know the significance of Red 40, so this functions as a plant/foreshadow that becomes funnier on rewatch. The timing of a child innocently requesting the conspiracy's MacGuffin mid-interrogation is a nice structural joke.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We ain't looking at you either.

jokes.text: Cricket? What are you doing here? / Dee paid me to cover her shift, hence the getup.
jokes.setup: Charlie finds Cricket in a suspicious location at the party
jokes.punchline: 'Hence the getup' — Cricket is apparently dressed in some kind of costume/uniform, the visual of Cricket in a ridiculous getup being the joke
jokes.explanation: Cricket's perpetually degraded status makes any getup inherently funny. The visual comedy is implied rather than described, so full impact is diminished in transcript form.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm no matador, Frank, so you can cut the bull.

jokes.text: More. Oh, yes. Do it. Harder. Yes. I'm a slut.
jokes.setup: Cricket is apparently performing some physical labor or task; Charlie asks why he was in the basement
jokes.punchline: Cricket is apparently moaning while doing work — his declaration 'I'm a slut' in response to whatever he's doing is simultaneously clarifying and more confusing
jokes.explanation: Cricket's self-aware degeneracy is well-deployed here. The escalating moans and 'I'm a slut' self-declaration is very Cricket — it's cringe comedy that works because the character has earned this level of depravity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Red 40.

jokes.text: Frank hired me to go down to the local bars and stick my fingers in the garnish stations.
jokes.setup: Cricket explains what Frank had him doing
jokes.punchline: The clinical description of deliberately contaminating bar garnishes with his fingers — delivered as if it's a reasonable job
jokes.explanation: Very Sunny in its specificity — 'stick my fingers in the garnish stations' is a disgusting yet precise image. Cricket's willingness to do this for money with no moral hesitation is perfect character work.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Ammonia-bleach cocktail, aka the Janitor's Helper. Luckily, I'm immune. I've built up a healthy tolerance over the years, or unhealthy, depending on how you look at it.

jokes.text: Why? / Why, to contaminate the cherries with feces, so people get sick, of course. / My God, that's disgusting. / It's an honest living.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks why Cricket was contaminating cherries
jokes.punchline: Cricket's matter-of-fact explanation followed by 'It's an honest living' — the disconnect between fecal contamination and 'honest living' is the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'it's an honest living' response to describing fecal contamination of cherries is a great joke — the total lack of irony in Cricket's self-assessment is very funny. This is exactly what Always Sunny does best: characters with broken moral compasses describing awful things with dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He's gonna wake up with his head pounding harder than a Chinese crossword puzzle. Huh? Was that... That one wasn't clear?

jokes.text: He flashed a roll of nickels, and I didn't ask questions. When someone flashes a roll of nickels at you, you don't ask questions, you just do. No matter what they want or where they want you to put it or where they want to put into you...
jokes.setup: Cricket explains why he didn't question Frank's instructions
jokes.punchline: The 'roll of nickels' as a motivating factor escalates into an increasingly dark implication about Cricket's willingness to do anything, ending with the dark 'where they want to put into you'
jokes.explanation: Cricket's escalating explanation of his own exploitation is both funny and dark — the 'roll of nickels' as a price point for anything is very character-specific. The trailing implication about 'where they want to put into you' pushes it into dark subversive territory that the show excels at.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, you put bleach on poison, it cancels it out, I'm pretty sure. No, it makes the poison more poisoning.

jokes.text: I'm gonna turn around now.
jokes.setup: Cricket's monologue about doing anything for a roll of nickels has gone to a very dark place
jokes.punchline: Charlie simply says 'I'm gonna turn around now' — a physical withdrawal from Cricket as a comedic beat
jokes.explanation: Perfectly timed comedic withdrawal. Five words, maximum impact. The physical implication (Charlie literally turning away from Cricket) combined with the matter-of-fact delivery makes this a very efficient joke.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: So that's why that shot I took wasn't vodka. It was bleach. The universal poison antidote.

jokes.text: Go kiss a duck. You'll never make me talk. / I'm not slapping you around again. / All right, fine, just get me a pen and I'll write 'em down.
jokes.setup: Cricket defiantly refuses to give up information — 'Go kiss a duck, you'll never make me talk'
jokes.punchline: Charlie mentions he's 'not slapping you around again' — implying prior violence — and Cricket immediately capitulates
jokes.explanation: Good two-beat joke. 'Go kiss a duck' is a funny period-appropriate insult, but the real laugh is Cricket's instant capitulation despite his bravado — the 'not slapping you around again' implies Charlie already broke him once offscreen. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I was undercover the whole time.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: I mean, what are you talking about? That doesn't even make sense.

jokes.text: So Cricket had contaminated the wrong guy's cherries and now Frank was dancing the porcelain rumba.
jokes.setup: Charlie narrates the accidental poisoning solution
jokes.punchline: 'Dancing the porcelain rumba' — a deliberately florid euphemism for being stuck on a toilet
jokes.explanation: 'The porcelain rumba' is a great noir euphemism — specific, evocative, and silly. The word 'rumba' is an inspired choice over 'tango' or similar, implying a lively, undignified movement.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Now I'm about to shit my brains all over this floor. But don't worry. I'll mop twice. I always do.

jokes.text: And there's only two things you can do in the dark: you can drink... and you can hide.
jokes.setup: Charlie reflects on being 'in the dark' about the case
jokes.punchline: His list of things to do in the dark — drink and hide — subverts the expected (drink and think, etc.) with the cowardly 'hide'
jokes.explanation: Good subversion of the brooding-detective-in-dark trope. 'You can hide' undermines whatever toughness Charlie has established. Character-consistent and economic.

jokes.text: If you came to shoot me, at least let me finish my drink first.
jokes.setup: Someone enters the bar; Charlie assumes the worst in full noir mode
jokes.punchline: His resigned acceptance of potential murder — provided he can finish his drink — is a great character beat
jokes.explanation: Classic noir fatalism applied to Charlie's alcoholism — the drink takes priority over survival. Well-executed if not particularly original.

jokes.text: I'm not gonna shoot you. What if I missed? / Well, then you'd have to say you missed me. / Maybe I did. / Maybe I missed you, too.
jokes.setup: The Waitress says she's not going to shoot Charlie
jokes.punchline: 'What if I missed?' / 'Then you'd have to say you missed me' — a pun on 'miss' as both marksmanship failure and emotional longing, which then gets played romantically
jokes.explanation: Clever wordplay with clean structure. The pun on 'missed' leads into a genuine romantic moment, which is unusually sweet for Always Sunny. The structure — setup, wordplay pivot, romantic sincerity — is well-constructed.

jokes.text: No, thanks. I'm sober. Plus, I saw you put cat food in it.
jokes.setup: Charlie offers the Waitress a drink
jokes.punchline: She refuses — not just because she's sober, but because she actually watched him put cat food in the drink
jokes.explanation: Excellent joke — the two-part refusal is perfectly constructed. 'I'm sober' is a reasonable excuse, but the real reveal is 'I saw you put cat food in it.' This is a perfect Charlie detail — his cat food obsession is a long-running show trait. The audience knows exactly why there's cat food in the drink, which makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Maybe I did, maybe I didn't. / You did, Charlie, I saw you scoop it out of the can. / I put a little bit in.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to maintain plausible deniability about the cat food
jokes.punchline: 'I put a little bit in' — the capitulation from denial to minimization, still not grasping why this is a problem
jokes.explanation: The progression from denial to 'I put a little bit in' is very Charlie — he never argues that cat food doesn't belong in drinks, only that the quantity was minimal. His lack of shame is the joke.

jokes.text: Goddamn it. Why are you smiling? / Well, I'm trying to look sexy. / You're supposed to be dead.
jokes.setup: Dee is apparently playing dead or some dramatic role in the story; she's doing it wrong
jokes.punchline: Charlie points out she's supposed to be dead; Dee insists she can be dead AND sexy
jokes.explanation: Good meta joke — the gang is apparently 'playing along' with Charlie's story but Dee can't resist trying to make herself look good even when playing a corpse. Very character-specific for Dee's vanity.

jokes.text: You're not supposed to be sexy. You're supposed to be the goon. / No, I'm not the goon. I don't want to be the goon. I want to be something better. / But you are the goon. / I'm not the goddamn goon. / You're the goon, Dee. Who else is the goon? You're the goon. / How could I be a goon? I'm wearing a nightie.
jokes.setup: Charlie tries to get Dee to play her assigned goon role; she resists
jokes.punchline: 'How could I be a goon? I'm wearing a nightie.' — Dee's argument that nightwear precludes goon status
jokes.explanation: The 'goon' running gag peaks here with Dee's escalating protest. 'How could I be a goon? I'm wearing a nightie' is a great absurd logic argument — the idea that nightwear confers protection from goon-status is very funny. The repetition of 'You're the goon' builds well.

jokes.text: Maybe that's your murder weapon. Take it off and you strangle...
jokes.setup: Dee argues the nightie prevents goon status
jokes.punchline: Mac suggests the nightie could be used as a murder weapon for strangling, making Dee even more dangerous
jokes.explanation: Decent riff — Mac's lateral thinking about the nightie-as-weapon is an unexpected tangent that adds chaos to the scene. Not particularly sharp but contributes to the energy.

jokes.text: He gives us 30%, only Mac thinks it's ten. / What? / Shut up!
jokes.setup: Dennis explains Frank's cherry scheme financial arrangement
jokes.punchline: Dennis casually reveals he's been cheating Mac on the split — in front of Charlie, then immediately tries to suppress it
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny — the gang casually betraying each other is a show staple. The timing of Dennis revealing this directly to Mac and then 'Shut up!' is perfectly executed. The nonchalance of the betrayal is the joke.

jokes.text: You talking to me? / Yeah. / Well, I can't tell 'cause I'm not looking at you. / We ain't looking at you either.
jokes.setup: Charlie addresses Mac and Dennis about Vince
jokes.punchline: The exchange about whether he's talking to them — none of them are looking at each other, in an apparently deliberate noir posture — is a visual comedy bit about masculine posturing
jokes.explanation: Good genre parody — the macho affectation of not making eye contact played for comedy. The mutual commitment to not looking at each other extends the joke well.

jokes.text: Are you still here? / No, we're gonna go now. / We're leaving now, though.
jokes.setup: After the conversation, there's apparently an awkward beat
jokes.punchline: Mac and Dennis's overlapping, redundant announcements of departure — 'No, we're gonna go now' / 'We're leaving now, though' — is a funny real-world comedy moment
jokes.explanation: The overlapping departure announcements capture an authentic human awkwardness — the two characters separately but simultaneously trying to escape. 'No, we're gonna go now' as an answer to 'Are you still here' is illogical but human.

jokes.text: Hey, is it, is it ten percent or is it really 30%?
jokes.setup: Mac and Dennis are leaving; Mac is still processing the cheating revelation
jokes.punchline: Mac stalls to ask the question he should have confronted immediately — the delayed indignation is funny
jokes.explanation: Good callback that shows Mac's delayed processing. His inability to let it go — asking on the way out the door — is a nice character beat showing his combination of pride and obliviousness.

jokes.text: Yeah, like a brick would explain gravity to my head.
jokes.setup: Charlie narrates his skepticism about Frank's offer to explain everything
jokes.punchline: 'Like a brick would explain gravity to my head' — the simile implies Frank's explanation will be delivered through physical violence
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. 'A brick would explain gravity to my head' is both genuinely poetic (gravity is explained to things that fall) and grimly funny (via getting hit with a brick). The image is vivid, specific, and original. High quotability — this is exactly the kind of line that elevates Charlie's noir narration above parody into something genuinely impressive.

jokes.text: No johns in the basement, pal.
jokes.setup: Charlie enters the bar to find Cricket; Frank is apparently absent
jokes.punchline: Cricket, in whatever capacity he's working, is policing the basement with 'No johns in the basement' — implying he's running some kind of operation down there
jokes.explanation: Cricket having authority over the basement of a bar and enforcing a 'no johns' rule is a funny implication — it suggests the full range of Cricket's activities. The confidence of the line is very character-specific.

jokes.text: My guts are cut to ribbons. / What? Who did this to you? / I did. I was carrying a jar of cherries, I fell on them, they bust, they sliced my stomach to bits.
jokes.setup: Frank appears gravely injured — 'my guts are cut to ribbons' — implying he was attacked
jokes.punchline: He did it to himself by falling on a jar of cherries — the elaborate injury is entirely self-inflicted by stupidity
jokes.explanation: Good misdirection — 'cut to ribbons' implies violence and conspiracy, but the self-inflicted stupidity of falling on cherries is a great deflation. Very Frank to have a dramatic injury from pure buffoonery.

jokes.text: I'm no matador, Frank, so you can cut the bull.
jokes.setup: Frank is trying to claim innocence about the cherry scam
jokes.punchline: 'I'm no matador, so you can cut the bull' — a noir version of 'cut the crap' that also riffs on the bull/matador metaphor
jokes.explanation: Clean wordplay with a visual image (matador/bull). 'Cut the bull' is an already-existing phrase made fresher by the matador setup. Good economy.

jokes.text: Old folks homes for pineapple upside-down cake, teenage birthday parties, and teetotalers who only drink Shirley Temples.
jokes.setup: Frank explains who was buying the black market cherries
jokes.punchline: The list of cherry buyers escalates from vaguely sympathetic (old folks, teens) to perfectly absurd (teetotalers who only drink Shirley Temples) — the last being both the most specific and funniest
jokes.explanation: Good escalating list structure. The specificity of 'teetotalers who only drink Shirley Temples' is excellent — it's a very particular niche of cherry dependency that Frank has identified and exploited. The image of organized crime targeting people who only drink mocktails is funny.

jokes.text: What is...? What-what is that? / Ammonia-bleach cocktail, aka the Janitor's Helper.
jokes.setup: Charlie has mixed something to use against Vince
jokes.punchline: 'Ammonia-bleach cocktail, aka the Janitor's Helper' — Charlie weaponizes his janitor knowledge, naming a toxic gas as a branded cocktail
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'The Janitor's Helper' as a branded name for a toxic gas cocktail is perfect — it's both a cleaning product parody (Mr. Clean, etc.) and a demonstration that Charlie's janitor expertise is actually his superpower in this noir. The confidence of naming it like a cocktail menu item is very funny. Highly quotable and high character integration.

jokes.text: Luckily, I'm immune. I've built up a healthy tolerance over the years, or unhealthy, depending on how you look at it.
jokes.setup: Charlie deploys the ammonia-bleach gas
jokes.punchline: He's immune — because he's inhaled so much ammonia bleach over the years that he's built a tolerance. The 'or unhealthy, depending on how you look at it' self-correction acknowledges this is actually terrible for him
jokes.explanation: Exceptional character joke. The reveal that Charlie is immune to toxic gas because he's inhaled it so much professionally is both a great plot twist and a devastating character detail. 'Or unhealthy, depending on how you look at it' is a perfect self-aware tag. This is the essence of the episode — Charlie's legitimate janitor skills are actually horrifying.

jokes.text: He's gonna wake up with his head pounding harder than a Chinese crossword puzzle. / Huh? / Was that... That one wasn't clear?
jokes.setup: Charlie delivers what he intends as a cool noir metaphor
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's confused 'Huh?' prompts Charlie to break character and admit 'That one wasn't clear?' — the metaphor didn't work and he knows it
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best meta moments. The whole episode has been Charlie perfecting his noir narration, and here one metaphor lands badly — 'Chinese crossword puzzle' doesn't quite work as an idiom — and he immediately breaks to workshop it. This is both a character moment (Charlie's self-awareness about his noir limitations) and a meta joke about the episode's conceit. Excellent craft.

jokes.text: Say, why didn't you tell me about Frank's cherry racket? / I don't know what you're talking about.
jokes.setup: Charlie asks the Waitress about her connection to the scheme; she denies it
jokes.punchline: This is a plant for the later reveal — in context it functions as a beat where the audience is set up to believe she's innocent
jokes.explanation: More of a plot beat than a joke on its own, but functions as setup for the reveal. Gets a rewatch bonus because on second viewing her obvious lie is more apparent.

jokes.text: There's nothing petty about you, is there, baby? / Ooh.
jokes.setup: The Waitress says she didn't want Charlie to think of her as a 'petty criminal'
jokes.punchline: Charlie's 'there's nothing petty about you' is meant romantically but is ironic since she IS in fact a criminal at a large scale (which the audience doesn't yet know)
jokes.explanation: Good dramatic irony — Charlie's compliment is unintentionally accurate in the wrong direction. Gets better on rewatch when you know she's the mastermind.

jokes.text: You idiot. I didn't tell you because it's my cherry racket.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just had a romantic moment with the Waitress and believes he's solved the case
jokes.punchline: The Waitress reveals she's the actual villain — 'it's my cherry racket' — completely subverting her sweet persona
jokes.explanation: Major tonal shift delivered with great economy. The 'you idiot' opener is perfect — it immediately signals the character change. The Waitress as the criminal mastermind is both a subversion of the femme fatale trope (she IS the villain, not just a pawn) and a great Always Sunny twist using an established character. The reveal also recontextualizes all prior scenes, making it funnier retroactively.

jokes.text: It was like shooting fish in a... / Charlie, are you still eating that pie? I poisoned it.
jokes.setup: The Waitress is mid-monologue explaining her scheme
jokes.punchline: She interrupts her own villain speech to tell Charlie he's eating a pie she poisoned — Charlie has been casually eating it throughout her revelation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a highlight of the entire episode. The structure is excellent: villain mid-monologue interrupted to tell the protagonist he's eating poison, while he continues to eat it. The 'it was like shooting fish in a...' incomplete cliché adds another layer of comedy. This is precisely calibrated slapstick/dark comedy with strong character integration — only Charlie would keep eating.

jokes.text: - You did? - Yeah, that's what I'm telling you. - Oh, yeah. You know what? There's a lot of threads going around; I'm losing track. - Okay, I poisoned the pie. - Yeah. - So you should stop eating it. - Right. / ...It's good. / - Thanks. Appreciate that. - Last bite.
jokes.setup: The Waitress has told Charlie the pie is poisoned; he acknowledges it
jokes.punchline: Charlie takes one more bite and says 'It's good,' then thanks her — a complete rejection of self-preservation in favor of enjoying a tasty pie
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie moment and arguably the best sustained comedic beat in the episode. The escalation is exquisite: (1) realization, (2) understanding, (3) taking one more bite, (4) complimenting the poison pie, (5) the Waitress's baffled 'Thanks. Appreciate that.' The 'There are a lot of threads going around' admission is also very funny — Charlie tracking this complex plot like it's just getting confusing. His prioritizing taste over survival is completely in character.

jokes.text: He figured out what I was up to and he wanted out, but we were making too much money, so I diarrhea-poisoned him to shut him up. / He got the message in the end.
jokes.setup: The Waitress explains how she handled Frank wanting out
jokes.punchline: 'I diarrhea-poisoned him to shut him up' — the word returns as a confirmed verb; 'He got the message in the end' is a dark pun (end = buttocks = diarrhea)
jokes.explanation: Excellent callback — 'diarrhea-poisoned' has now been elevated to a verb used by the actual villain. 'He got the message in the end' is a solid dark pun. The word's journey through the episode gives it a satisfying payoff.

jokes.text: Oh, Vince caught me smuggling boozy pies into A.A. and threatened to rat me out to my parole officer. You see, he wasn't actually my boyfriend. He was my sponsor, and he was a real buzzkill, literally.
jokes.setup: The Waitress explains Vince's real role
jokes.punchline: Vince was her AA sponsor, not her boyfriend — and 'a real buzzkill, literally' is both a pun (he literally kills the buzz of the boozy pies) and dark (she knocked him out)
jokes.explanation: Good reveal with a satisfying pun payoff. 'Boozy pies into A.A.' is a great crime concept, and 'real buzzkill, literally' works on two levels. The sponsor-not-boyfriend twist recontextualizes earlier scenes effectively.

jokes.text: So that's why that shot I took wasn't vodka. It was bleach. / What? / The universal poison antidote. / No, it's not. / It's not? / I mean, if anything, you've ingested more poison. / No, you put bleach on poison, it cancels it out, I'm pretty sure. / No, it makes the poison more poisoning. / No. The two things cancel... / No, you're right. Here come the cherries.
jokes.setup: Charlie reveals he drank bleach thinking it was a universal antidote
jokes.punchline: The 'debate' about whether bleach cancels poison ends with 'No, you're right. Here come the cherries.' — an immediate physical consequence confirming the Waitress's correct medical knowledge
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's absolute best sequences. Multiple layers: (1) Charlie's insane belief that bleach is a universal antidote, (2) the calm back-and-forth debate about basic chemistry, (3) his refusal to accept correct information, (4) the immediate physical proof via vomiting cherries. 'Here come the cherries' is a perfect button — it's simultaneous comedy and callback to the entire cherry plot. The character integration is exceptional: only Charlie would drink bleach as a medical intervention. Very high impact, very quotable.

jokes.text: Oh, God! / Jesus Christ, Charlie!
jokes.setup: Charlie has just vomited cherries on or near the Waitress
jokes.punchline: The Waitress's horrified reaction to being in the blast radius of cherry-vomit
jokes.explanation: Physical reaction beat — the horror of being vomited on after a poisoning is funny. Less craft than the preceding joke, but the visual implied by 'Jesus Christ, Charlie!' lands as a good physical beat.

jokes.text: Either way, you're done, baby doll. I called the cops to take you downtown. / Ha ha! / The gig's up, you ugly dame. You're under arrest. / What the hell? I was undercover the whole time. I mean, what are you talking about? / Yeah, I switched things up.
jokes.setup: The villain is apparently cornered; then Dee appears to make an arrest
jokes.punchline: Dee claims she was 'undercover the whole time' — which makes no sense given everything we've seen, and 'I switched things up' is her only explanation
jokes.explanation: Good payoff for Dee's arc — she's been saddled with 'goon' status all episode and asserts agency by claiming she was undercover. The 'I switched things up' as her only justification is very Dee. It makes no narrative sense, which is part of the joke.

jokes.text: Got tired of being called a goon. Let's go!
jokes.setup: Dee explains why she went 'undercover'
jokes.punchline: 'Got tired of being called a goon' — the entire episode's running gag is revealed as Dee's character motivation
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the episode's central running gag. 'Got tired of being called a goon' as the actual motivation for Dee's character actions is both funny and surprisingly human. It resolves the goon arc with maximum efficiency (five words) while also being completely in character for Dee's vanity. The whole goon thread pays off beautifully here.

jokes.text: - You're really hurting my arm. - Yeah, that's okay with me. / - This is so stupid! Let go of me! - All right. / No, I'm not gonna let go of you. I got one job to do, I'm gonna finish it.
jokes.setup: Dee is arresting the Waitress — apparently rougher than necessary
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah, that's okay with me' in response to 'you're really hurting my arm' shows Dee's complete indifference — she's enjoying the power — and 'I got one job to do, I'm gonna finish it' adds dignity to something comically excessive
jokes.explanation: Dee's relish in finally having authority after being the goon all episode is funny. The seriousness of 'I got one job to do' applied to what appears to be an unnecessary roughing is good character work.

jokes.text: It's not every day that a janitor makes his own mess, but when he does... ooh, boy. Now I'm about to shit my brains all over this floor.
jokes.setup: Charlie delivers his closing narration
jokes.punchline: 'Now I'm about to shit my brains all over this floor' — the whole janitor/mess metaphor pays off with a literal, graphic version: Charlie is about to have his own diarrhea incident from the poison pie
jokes.explanation: Perfect closer. The whole episode has built to this — the janitor who solves a diarrhea-poisoning case is about to become the victim of diarrhea-poisoning himself. The 'makes his own mess' line elegantly connects the noir metaphor to the literal. 'Shit my brains all over this floor' is graphic but earns it through the structural setup. The 'ooh, boy' pause is perfect timing.

jokes.text: But don't worry. I'll mop twice. I always do.
jokes.setup: Charlie has just announced he's about to defecate on the bar floor
jokes.punchline: 'I'll mop twice. I always do.' — the episode title payoff; Charlie's tragic professionalism is to clean up his own mess
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the stronger episode endings in Always Sunny. 'I'll mop twice. I always do.' is the episode title, the thesis statement, and the punchline all in one — it crystallizes the entire structural joke of the episode (Charlie the janitor-noir-detective) while delivering the darkest possible version of professionalism. The economy is perfect (six words), the character integration is perfect (only Charlie), and the structural payoff earns the highest score. This is very close to anchor-caliber writing.

tmdb_overview: In the black-and-white noir world of his memory, Charlie navigates the seedy underbelly of Philadelphia as Frank has been "diarrhea poisoned," and it's up to Charlie to clean up the mess.
